one_liner: Tiny npm package: hand-written WAT f32x4 SIMD dot product and cosine similarity, faster than JS cosine libraries on Float32Array input.
what_it_does: Exports two functions: normalize(vec) returns an L2-normalized Float32Array copy, and getSimilarity(a, b, {normalize?}) returns the dot product (cosine similarity if both inputs are already unit length) or, with {normalize: true}, a full cosine similarity computed inside WebAssembly. Inputs may be Float32Array or number[] (number[] since 0.2.0). It is not a drop-in for the baseline libraries: the default call skips normalization, results are f32 rather than f64, and length mismatches are not checked.
how_it_is_fast: The kernel is about 200 lines of hand-written WebAssembly text using 128-bit f32x4 multiply and add, unrolled 4x with four independent accumulators (16 floats per iteration) and a scalar tail, embedded as a sub-1 KB base64 module. Pre-normalizing once lets each comparison be a single dot-product pass instead of the three running sums a cosine needs. Each call still copies both vectors into a module-global WebAssembly.Memory with Float32Array.set, so the README's 'zero-copy' wording is inaccurate.
when_to_use: Brute-force similarity over embedding vectors (384 to 1536 dims and up) kept as Float32Array and normalized once at insert time, where each query is many dot products.
Browser or Node code that wants WASM SIMD speed without a build step or native addon; the whole package is a 2.4 KB ESM file plus a UMD build.
Larger dimensions: in this enrichment's Node 22 runs the dot-only path was 3.3-4x faster than a plain JS dot-product loop at 1536 dims, but only 1.5-2x at 384 dims.
when_not_to_use: Inputs held as plain number[] arrays: each call converts them with new Float32Array(...), and in this enrichment that made getSimilarity 7-20x slower than cos-similarity on the same number[] input (0.11M vs 2.25M ops/s at 384 dims, 0.07M vs 0.51M at 1536), the opposite of the README claim.

Code that feeds the result to Math.acos to get an angle (the package's name): f32 rounding returned self-similarities above 1 (up to 1.00000036) for 594 of 2,000 normalized random vectors, which gives NaN unless you clamp.
Callers that need f64 accuracy or validation: the JS baselines accumulate in doubles and two of them check types and lengths; fast-theta returns f32 and does neither.
Runtimes without WebAssembly SIMD (older Safari before 16.4, old Node): there is no scalar fallback, so module instantiation fails.
Large-scale k-NN search: it compares one pair per call with a JS-to-WASM copy each time; a batched or indexed vector library avoids the per-call copy (the author points to Eigen DB for kNN).

integration.form: npm module (ESM and UMD builds with the WASM inlined as base64)
integration.min_toolchain: Any JS runtime with WebAssembly SIMD (fixed-width 128-bit) support, e.g. Node 16.4+, Chrome 91+, Firefox 89+, Safari 16.4+; building from source needs wabt and vite
integration.thread_safety: Module-global WebAssembly memory reused by every call; safe in single-threaded JS, so each worker gets its own instance
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — getSimilarity(a, b, {normalize: true}) gives a cosine similarity like cos-similarity(a, b), but in f32, with no length check and a different signature; the default call is only a dot product

gotchas: Mismatched lengths fail silently or throw, depending on order: dims comes from the first vector, so after an earlier call with longer vectors, getSimilarity(ones(8), ones(4)) returned 8 in this enrichment (stale wasm memory filled the missing half; zero-padding would give 4), while getSimilarity(ones(4), ones(8)) throws 'RangeError: offset is out of bounds'.

The README headline row is the dot-only path on pre-normalized Float32Array input, compared with full cosine similarity in the JS libraries on number[] input. The fair 'with normalize' row is in the repo's bench but missing from the README; in this enrichment it was 1.3x cos-similarity at 384 dims (2.89M vs 2.25M ops/s) and 2.2x at 1536 (1.13M vs 0.51M).
A zero vector is left unnormalized and gives similarity 0 rather than NaN or an error; fast-cosine-similarity throws ZeroVectorError in the same case.

Most of the code was written by GitHub Copilot agent PRs (#1 for the core library, #2 for number[] support) over two days in February 2026; there is no LICENSE file in the repo, only "license": "MIT" in package.json and on npm.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Like kmeans-wasm (wasm k-means vs skmeans) and hash-wasm (wasm hashing vs pure-JS hash libraries), it replaces a pure-JS npm numeric routine with WASM; pick fast-theta only for single-pair cosine or dot products on Float32Array embeddings, where it is the smallest option (under 1 KB of WASM, no dependencies).
verified_claims_summary: The README reports vitest bench numbers in Node on an unstated CPU and Node version: fast-theta's dot-only path on pre-normalized Float32Array reached 3.3M/2.6M/1.8M ops/s at 384/768/1536 dims, against 1.8M/1.1M/597K for cos-similarity 2.0.0 and slower figures for fast-cosine-similarity 1.2.2 and compute-cosine-similarity 1.1.0, all computing full cosine on number[] input. Re-running the published 0.2.0 package on Node 22.22.0 (Intel Xeon 2.10 GHz cloud vCPU, isolated process per row, best of 5) reproduced the shape: 4.29M vs cos-similarity 2.25M at 384 dims and 2.47M vs 0.51M at 1536. The like-for-like {normalize: true} row was 1.3x and 2.2x faster, a plain JS dot product on the same pre-normalized Float32Array reached 2.06-2.92M and 0.62-0.72M ops/s, and number[] input made fast-theta 7-20x slower than the baselines (numbers measured in this enrichment, not by the project).
status_note: Small single-author npm package (0.2.0, published 2026-02-27; 25 commits, 1 star, no activity since): MIT per package.json, small enough to copy as one WAT file, and correct for equal-length Float32Array inputs, but treat it as a Float32Array-only helper.
